source.title: MoE Sparsity Begets Monosemanticity: Insights into Understanding and Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Ming-Xue Tian; Qi Zhang; Xiao-Han Wang; Jia-Jun Chai; Guo-Jun Yin; Wei Lin; Cai-Lian Chen; Qi-Min Xu; Si-Yu Wang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The paper applies an explanation-and-activation-prediction framework to neurons in one selected layer and reports qualitative neuron explanations, a different measurement from the original sources. Its main quantitative monosemanticity results are for MoE experts, not individual neurons.
record.gate_note: The paper's main findings concern expert-level monosemanticity, so those results do not directly test claims about individual neurons. Appendix A.10 separately applies the framework to neurons and reports example explanations, but does not estimate the prevalence of polysemantic neurons. Fine-tuning benchmark results are not rows because they measure downstream task performance, not neuron polysemanticity. The word-limit and evaluator comparisons measure expert-level scores and are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study measures expert-level monosemanticity in MoE models, a different unit from individual neurons. Its only neuron-level material is six unscored example explanations from one expert in one selected layer (Appendix A.10, Table 8). It gives no neuron prevalence, no neuron scores and no test of whether neuron inputs are unrelated, so it tests no version. The sparsity, layer and word-limit results are expert-level, a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors also conclude that their monosemanticity-guided expert-frozen fine-tuning (EDMRS) matches or beats full fine-tuning in-domain while better preserving out-of-domain performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses natural-language expert/neuron explanations followed by an external LLM's activation predictions, rather than the original sources' neuron-level visualizations and related interpretability analyses. The paper's main method is designed for MoE experts.
record.method_sensitivity: Expert LDS varies with routing sparsity, layer, evaluator, and explanation word limit. The paper reports a general trend across sparsity values and layer depth; evaluator correlations are 0.815 and 0.774, human agreement is 0.701, and the 20-word limit gives the highest reported LDS among tested explanation limits.

fits_no_version.finding: Reducing MoE routing sparsity (raising k) lowers expert-level LDS across the four evaluated layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher MoE routing sparsity is associated with stronger expert-level monosemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert LDS rises rapidly in early layers, plateaus high in middle layers and drops sharply near the output in Qwen3-235B-A22B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE expert monosemanticity peaks in middle layers.

fits_no_version.finding: EDMS is generally lower than EMS. The authors identify polysemantic experts active across multiple domains alongside domain-specialized experts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE models contain both polysemantic (cross-domain) and domain-specialized experts.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert LDS rankings correlate with alternative evaluators (Spearman 0.815, 0.774) and with human judgments (Spearman 0.701).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-level monosemanticity scores are fairly robust to evaluator choice.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert LDS varies modestly with explanation word limit (0.6869 to 0.7081), highest at 20 words.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert monosemanticity scores depend somewhat on explanation length.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
record.problems: The neuron comparison is a qualitative case study from one selected intermediate layer and does not estimate neuron-level polysemanticity prevalence. The main monosemanticity results concern experts. Several score trends are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The framework relies on LLM-generated explanations and LLM activation predictions, though the paper reports evaluator and human-annotator correlations.
record.rows_left_out: No downstream benchmark rows were included because they report fine-tuning performance rather than neuron or expert monosemanticity. No cited results from other studies were included.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons and no layer comparison at neuron level; there are only six qualitative neuron explanations.
Superposition as the cause of neuron polysemanticity is not tested.
Initialization, regularization and noise as causes are not tested.
Routing sparsity is varied only for expert-level scores, not for the neuron polysemantic share; there is no activation-function or regularization comparison.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons are misread generalization is not examined.
The word-limit and evaluator sensitivity results concern expert scores only; there is no neuron activation-range analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Neuron explanations r1-r4 are shifted by one position relative to Table 8; the text of A.10 confirms Neuron 131 is the angle-bracket explanation. The study does not test any neuron-level version. Its expert-level sparsity result is only an analogue of V5, measured on experts rather than neurons.

versions.untested_parts: Image classifiers and InceptionV1 neuron responses.

The study provides qualitative examples from neurons in one selected layer, but does not measure what share of transformer MLP neurons are polysemantic, compare layers for neuron polysemanticity, or assess prevalence across models.
The study discusses MoE sparsity and expert monosemanticity, but does not test neuron polysemanticity as a consequence of representing more sparse features than available neurons.
Initialization, regularization, and training-noise explanations for neuron polysemanticity are not tested.

The study varies MoE routing sparsity for expert-level scores, not neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings; it does not test lowering neuron polysemanticity against performance cost.
The study does not determine whether canonical neuron mixtures share a feature or related job, or whether truly unrelated neuron mixtures are rare.
The study varies explanation word limits for expert-level scores, but does not test neuron polysemanticity across activation ranges or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Neuron 131 (within Expert 114)
rows.operation_detail: Generated a natural-language explanation from neuron activation examples using the monosemanticity framework.

conditions.value: randomly selected intermediate layer described as monosemantic

rows.measure: Qualitative neuron explanation of activation examples.
rows.value: Explanation characterized activations as short function words and suffixes within word fragments.
rows.note: The paper says neuron explanations operate at a lower semantic level than expert explanations. One example does not establish whether a large share of neurons respond to unrelated contexts.
rows.check: Value is misaligned with Table 8. Per A.10 and Table 8, Neuron 131's explanation is words between '<' and '>' symbols, not short function words and suffixes. It is a single unscored qualitative explanation and cannot show polysemanticity or its prevalence.

rows.measure: Qualitative neuron explanation of activation examples.
rows.value: Explanation characterized activations as numerical values, percentages, and mathematical or quantitative indicators.
rows.note: A qualitative example; the paper does not report whether this is a common neuron pattern or whether the listed activations are unrelated.
rows.check: Value is misaligned. In Table 8, Neuron 710 is described as short function words and suffixes within word fragments; the numerical-values explanation belongs to Neuron 419. Unscored qualitative example.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Varied MoE routing sparsity by changing the number of experts activated per token and measured layer-wise decoupling score (LDS).

conditions.value: varied k; exact values not stated

rows.measure: Layer-wise decoupling score (LDS), the layer average of expert monosemanticity scores (EMS).
rows.value: Text reports that reducing sparsity consistently and substantially decreases LDS across all evaluated layers; Figure 3a gives the plotted values.
rows.note: This is an expert-level result, not a measurement of individual-neuron polysemanticity. Exact plotted values are not stated in the text.

rows.subject: Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Measured layer-wise expert LDS across network depth.

conditions.value: network depth; individual layer values not stated

rows.value: Text reports a rapid early increase, a high middle-layer plateau, and a sharp decline near the output.
rows.note: The result concerns expert scores, not neuron-level prevalence.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Measured general EMS and domain-specific EDMS for experts using explanation generation and activation prediction.
rows.measure: Expert monosemanticity scores (EMS and EDMS) and qualitative activation patterns.
rows.baseline: EMS compared with EDMS; exact score values not stated in text.
rows.value: Text reports EDMS scores are generally lower than EMS scores and describes both domain-specialized experts and experts activated across multiple domains.
rows.note: The authors explicitly report polysemantic experts, but this is expert-level evidence and does not measure neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Qwen3-235B-A22B
rows.operation_detail: Recomputed layer-wise LDS profiles with alternative external LLM evaluators and correlated them with original scores.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation with original LDS scores.
rows.note: This tests evaluator consistency for expert-level scores, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Qwen3-235B-A22B

rows.note: This validates expert-level scoring; the correlation does not measure neuron polysemanticity.
